assumptions.text: Audiences expect clarity and coherence in spoken narratives, especially in educational or performative contexts.
Self-preservation overrides ideological purity in survival scenarios involving marginalized groups.
Historical trauma is best understood through extended metaphors and allegorical frameworks.
Racial identities are maintained through systemic erasure and selective mythmaking by dominant cultural institutions.
Power dynamics in media production reflect broader societal hierarchies and serve to reinforce existing dominance structures.
Narratives about race and history should prioritize lived experience and emotional truth over strict factual accuracy.
The concept of 'heroic struggle' requires supporting layers of conflict and complexity to remain compelling.
Cultural criticism can be effectively communicated through informal, conversational language and personal anecdotes.
Sexualized representations in media function as tools of psychological warfare and identity destabilization.
Truth in discourse emerges from collective reflection and shared recognition, not singular authoritative voices.
